verses.1: Al-Mizan defines tasbih as declaring God transcendent and free from every defect, and the present tense indicates its continuity. Malik is authority over a social order; Quddus is intensified purity; Aziz is unconquerable might; and Hakim is perfection in action, free of aimlessness and ignorance. These names are the proof-like introduction to the Messenger's raising in (62:2). Created things, by their own deficiencies and needs, declare the One who completes deficiencies and meets needs to be free of both. As King, He has the right to govern creation and legislate for His servants, whose duty is obedience. Religion and worship do not answer a divine need, for the Holy is need-free; human refusal does not defeat the Mighty; and the Wise cannot legislate futilely. His commands return benefit to creatures by setting their worldly and otherworldly condition right. Thus revelation, recitation, purification, and teaching through the Messenger are pure favor and grace, and grounds for glorifying Him.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes ummiyyun principally as those who do not read or write, namely the Arabs among whom Muhammad arose. This describes his origin, not a restriction of his mission to Arabs: the revelation first addressed them in their language, and when the call was established he summoned Jews, Christians, Magians, kings, and chiefs. The alternative that it means people without a scripture is unsuitable because the Prophet did not reserve recitation of the verses to them; the identification with Meccans is likewise remote from the Medinan context. Abraham and Ishmael's prayer in (2:128) and (2:129), for Ishmael's Arab descendants generally, corroborates this reading. The Messenger recites God's communications despite being unlettered, purifies the community, and teaches the Book and wisdom. Purification is wholesome, blessed human growth through virtuous morals and righteous deeds, making life and death upright. Teaching the Book includes its wording and the explanation of its obscure verses; wisdom is the real knowledge in the Qur'an. In this account of actual prophetic nurture, purification precedes teaching because it prepares people for true knowledge; in Abraham's prayer, which speaks of their eventual realization, knowledge and wisdom take precedence in rank over moral action. Their prior condition was emphatically manifest error.

verses.4: Al-Mizan identifies the grace as the sending of Muhammad to recite the signs, purify, and teach the Book and wisdom. The distal demonstrative magnifies this bestowal: God chose Muhammad for it, and may also be understood as choosing both the Messenger and the community to whom he was sent, which explains why he is from among them. The verse and its predecessors are an invocation of gratitude for this grace, which belongs to God alone and is granted as He wills.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan says those charged with the Torah were charged with its teachings, and bearing it means acting upon them. The Jews received from Moses its wisdom and laws but abandoned its demands. They are therefore like a donkey carrying books: the books may disclose realities, but the animal knows none of their knowledge or wisdom and gains only the burden's fatigue.

The preferred connection returns to this chapter's favor to Muslims: the unlettered Messenger draws them from error to knowledge and wisdom. The chapter later rebukes Muslims who left the Friday sermon for trade and diversion, belittling a major ritual. The Torah parable warns them not to repeat the Jews' failure to honor and act upon what they knew; they must revere the Messenger and their religion lest they earn a comparable divine wrath. Alusi's alternative, that the parable mainly targets those who recognized the foretold unlettered Prophet in the Torah but rejected him, is reported as arbitrary and unsupported by context.
verses.6: Al-Mizan treats the command to Jews to invoke death as a test exposing the falsity of their exclusive claim to be God's favorites, reflected in (5:18), (2:94), and (2:111). One who loves God and is certain of Paradise should desire the meeting with Him; death alone stands between him and that abode of dignity, whereas worldly life is full of sorrow and adversity. The phrasing favorites for God rather than God's favorites may itself mark their claim as unsupported by divine reality.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says the addressed Jews will never invoke death because their prior oppression, injustice, and evil make them dread meeting God. Their refusal proves that they are neither His friends nor lovers, while God fully knows the unjust. The two verses repeat in meaning (2:94) and (2:95), and the editorial note confines the pronoun to the Jews addressed in the Prophet's time, not every Jew.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reads the conditional result as a threat: the death from which the Jews flee will certainly meet them. Their abhorrence of it is linked to the punishment their evil deeds entail. They will then return to the Lord whose worship they abandoned and whose opposition they enacted, the Knower of unseen and seen, who will disclose their deeds and their evil consequences. The verse thus affirms death's inevitability, return and accountability, full recompense, and God's knowledge of every public and hidden deed; their deception cannot evade Him.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies the Friday call as the adhan and the commanded prayer as the legislated Friday prayer. Sa'y is earnest, quick going. Remembrance may mean the prayer or the sermon before it, but the command to leave trade in context forbids everything that keeps a person from the prayer, trade being its most obvious case. The order therefore requires believers to hasten diligently to the Friday observance and abandon all competing preoccupations; calling this better encourages obedience.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says that after the Friday prayer people may disperse and seek God's grace. The permission is not confined to commerce: it includes all gifts and rewarding works, such as visiting the sick, meeting a believer's need, visiting fellow believers, and attending knowledge sessions. Because dispersal follows the preceding prohibition, its imperative signifies permission rather than obligation, as do seek and remember. Abundant remembrance includes inward turning of the heart, not speech alone. It removes heedlessness, settles the remembered meaning in the soul, produces piety and God-consciousness, and so yields the success here defined by purification and knowledge and deliverance from every misery.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan reports a Shi'a and Sunni agreement that a Friday caravan arrived while the Prophet was standing in the pre-prayer sermon, and its drum and tambourine caused the congregants to scatter toward it, leaving him almost alone; the verse was revealed over that event. Lahw is the musical entertainment used to gather people for trade. The feminine pronoun in they hastened to it most naturally returns to the feminine noun trade, the caravan's actual aim, although it may grammatically refer to either trade or sport because either can occasion the rush and the verbal noun lahw can take feminine reference.

What is with God is the reward of hearing the sermon and its exhortation. It is better separately than sport and than trade because it is real, enduring good, whereas their good is fanciful, fleeting, futile, and may, in the case of sport, incur wrath. The comparative may simply mean good rather than a balance of equal goods. The shift from direct address to third person heightens the reproof: God declines to honor those who did this with direct address, and even the command to the Prophet leaves them unnamed. God is the Best of sustainers, one of His beautiful names.
